title: 'I could never hear on my left side - until I got a prosthetic ear'
content:
Imagine being born without an ear and spending your entire life without being able to hear on one side.
Stephen Gilbert, 74, from Aghalee, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side.
But he was recently fitted with a newly-designed prosthesis that accommodates a hearing aid, allowing him to hear on his left side for the first time.
That's thanks to oral and maxillofacial surgery at the Ulster Hospital; the only service of its kind in Northern Ireland, providing bespoke prostheses for people affected by birth defects, traumatic injuries and cancer surgery.
"To be able to hear someone on my left that I could never do before is just very special," Gilbert said.
"It's a huge thing to be able to have a prosthetic part of your face."
"In my case with an ear, it's not just as visual as someone maybe needing a prosthetic for the front part of their face, maybe through injury or through cancer," he added.
"I'm very conscious of that, but I'm very grateful for what has happened to me."
Growing up during the 1960s, when boys commonly wore their hair long, Gilbert could cover the area where his ear should have been.
But he became increasingly conscious of his condition as he grew older, particularly as hairstyles changed and his hair became thinner.
Gilbert first attended the Ulster Hospital in October 1997 for a prosthetic ear and over the past 29 years has had artificial ears made, repaired and adapted.
Previously, plastic surgery had attempted to reconstruct "some semblance of an ear" using skin and tissue taken from other parts of his body, but the results could not replicate the shape of a natural ear.
But after his wife read a magazine article about advances in prosthetics, describing how they had progressed from basic skin grafts to realistic artificial ears, Gilbert went to his GP.
"I'd managed for so long, but I suppose I knew that the hair wasn't always going to be there and something needed to be done," he said.
The previous grafted tissue was then removed and small implants were inserted to support the artificial ear.
A mould of his right ear was then used to create a matching left ear, before getting the colour and fit right.
"Amazing, that I had something that I didn't have there before.
"That was just remarkable," he said.
His new prosthetic ear holds a hearing aid which transmits sounds from his left side to his functioning ear.
The prosthesis has helped Gilbert feel less self-conscious when his ear is exposed, while advances in hearing aids have also made a "huge difference" to his life.

title: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung cancer
content: Pope Leo XIV had surgery Tuesday at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in northwest Rome to remove a nodule that was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. The Vatican said surgeons removed the cancerous growth, along with the lower lobe of his right lung. Pulmonary adenocarcinoma accounts for about 40% of all lung cancer cases. It’s a form of non-small cell lung cancer, and it usually grows and spreads to other parts of the body more slowly than small cell lung cancer does. Surgery is typically the first step when someone has this form of cancer. The right lung, which is larger, has three sections called lobes, and the left has two; doctors will often remove the lobe the growth is found in to get rid of the tumor and to improve chances of a cure. The body eventually adapts to compensate for this loss of function. It’s not always clear what causes this type of lung cancer. Although smoking can raise the risk, other risk factors include exposure to radon gas – the most common cause of lung cancer other than smoking – and particle pollution. Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is most often diagnosed in people who have never smoked. It is also more common in women, younger patients and people of East Asian ancestry. Adenocarcinoma is a leading cause of cancer-related death because doctors often don’t discover it until it’s at an advanced stage. But on Sunday, the pope told a crowd that doctors had detected a growth in his lungs at “a very early stage.” Based on what we know now, the pope should have a good prognosis, said Dr. Juanita Mora , the national medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association. “The fact that Pope Leo had a localized case of adenocarcinoma with an early-stage detection works in his favor,” Mora said. “Especially after surgical removal.” Mora said Leo’s recovery may be a “little bit longer” because the lungs will have to adjust to the removal of one lobe. “Initially, it will be a little harder for him to breathe until the left lung starts to compensate for it,” Mora said. Having lessened lung capacity may not make much of a difference for his breathing. Working in his favor, Mora said, is that the pope is not a smoker and is an otherwise healthy 71-year-old who plays tennis and exercises his lungs. Mora said he will have to do respiratory therapy exercises . He also will need to be careful to avoid respiratory infections as best he can because they could affect him more without part of his lung. She noted that Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, also had a lobectomy on his right side after a severe tuberculosis infection when he was young. “So obviously, a lot of people live and can fully do everything in terms of function and capacity, even with a lobectomy.” After this type of surgery, patients normally remain hospitalized for a few days until their vital signs and oxygen levels are stable, then typically continue recovering at home. Because it was a lobectomy, some pain is also expected. Whether Leo can take a planned trip to Latin America next month will depend on what tests find in the next few days, Mora said. In these cases, doctors examine samples from the lymph nodes around the lung, in addition to lung tissue, to determine the stage of the adenocarcinoma. Cancerous cells in the lymph nodes or any sign that the cancer has spread would help determine whether the pope needs treatment beyond surgery, such as chemotherapy or radiation. Doctors also will conduct genetic and biomarker testing to determine how to treat the cancer further, if necessary. Knowing a person’s particular biomarkers can help target immunotherapy if needed. Biomarker testing has significantly improved lung cancer treatment, Mora added, but in the US, only 15 states require medical insurers to cover such testing, even when someone has lung cancer. “We’re hoping, though, that it’s just an isolated cancer where he’s one and done, in which now we see a survival rate of 80% to 98% when it comes to surgical removal,” Mora said of Leo. “But now we will have to wait for these tests.”

title: Could GLP-1 drugs be anti-aging medications?
content: GLP-1 medications for weight loss and diabetes appear to slow the body’s aging processes, a sign that the blockbuster drugs could ultimately help people live longer. The idea that these medications may extend lifespan isn’t exactly far-fetched; it’s more of an extension of what they’ve already been shown to do. Studies have found that along with helping people shed fat and control blood sugar, GLP-1 drugs improve the health of many different parts of the body, lowering the risk of heart, kidney and liver disease, for example, and reducing sleep apnea and inflammation, which contribute to loss of health and function as people age. “Aging is the biggest risk factor for many diseases, and if we can target aging itself, we might be able to treat all kinds of diseases that are associated with aging,” said Dr. Danica Chen, a professor at the University of California at Berkeley who studies calorie restriction and aging. Now, scientists have turned their attention to biological markers of aging to better understand exactly how GLP-1 drugs may affect the aging process. The new research conducted in mice and people is early, and scientists say they don’t know whether the benefits apply only to people who are overweight or have diabetes when they start taking them medications, or if they could also slow aging in people who are normal weight and otherwise healthy. For that reason, experts say it’s too early for people to use this medication solely in the hopes of living longer. “There are people who are biohacking and taking these agents who are not either diabetic or obese, and the question there is what happens in lean younger non-diabetic individuals, especially over the long term,” said Dr. James Kirkland, who directs the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. “My concern is that people could overread some of this stuff.” Kirkland says the metrics used in the new studies – which are based on measurements of epigenetics, the way genes are turned on and off in the body and the measures of proteins our bodies make over time — are still in development, and although they’re useful for studies in larger groups of people, they’re not very informative for individuals, though many companies have begun marketing these types of tests to curious consumers. “They can vary tremendously from day to day within a person,” Kirkland said. Still, these early findings are generating excitement. “We’re seeing a reduction in age,” somewhere around three to six years, said Dr. Kevin Duffin, vice president of aging research at Eli Lilly. Lilly makes tirzepatide, which is sold as Zepbound for weight loss and Mounjaro for diabetes management. “It’s not the panacea. It’s not like we’re going to reduce age by 30 years or something, but it’s a significant reduction,” Duffin told a packed audience at the recent Aging Research and Drug Discovery conference in Boston. Duffin presented new data from Lilly’s Surmount V clinical trial, which randomly assigned more than 700 adults who were overweight but did not have diabetes to use either tirzepatide or semaglutide for 72 weeks. The aging study looked at a group of 71 participants from the study who were on tirzepatide and over the age of 50. By measuring how certain genes in their blood were turned off and on during the course of the study, the researchers were able to look at changes to so-called epigenetic clocks, which reveal the biological age of their organs and tissues, as opposed to their calendar age. Over the course of the study, Duffin explained, they would have expected a person to age 1.38 years in chronological time. But in the small group of study participants who were using tirzepatide, biological clocks advanced more slowly. Across different types of epigenetic clocks, the researchers saw an average change of between 1.1 years and 0.7 years in biological aging. Some biological clocks actually went backward, suggesting that some organs and tissues were acting younger than when people started the study. Duffin acknowledged that the study has limitations. There was no placebo group who were not using any weight loss meds to compare against the people on tirzepatide, for example, and the follow-up was relatively brief. From what the researchers could see, the anti-aging effects seemed to get stronger over time, however, so they hope to follow people for longer in the next trial. “Be very interesting to see what happens at four or five years after treatment with a GLP-1,” Duffin said. It’s also not yet clear whether the slowing of the biological aging is due to weight loss or if there could be some effect of the GLP-1 drugs independently. There’s a lot of good evidence, for example, that eating a calorie-restricted diet — cutting calories by about 25% — has anti-aging effects and extends the lifespan of many types of animals. Studies have shown that weight loss surgery, which helps people drop significant amounts of weight, slows biological aging, too. But it’s very hard to achieve weight loss or cut calories that much through willpower alone, making the role of medications and surgery critical. In one of the first questions after his talk, an audience member asked Duffin whether he had repeated the experiment in someone who was not overweight, to see if the effect was a result of weight loss or something else the drug was doing. “We get this question all the time,” Duffin said. “The bottom line is, these drugs work through [blood sugar] reduction and through weight loss, and the effects we’re seeing are mostly due to that.” The drug semaglutide, which is sold as Wegovy and Ozempic, shows many of the same anti-aging benefits, according to new research from drugmaker Novo Nordisk. By measuring changes to proteins in the body over time in people using semaglutide, the company’s scientists found that it reduced the heart’s biological age by two to four years compared with a placebo, and it reduced the age of organs such as the lung, kidney, brain and pancreas by one to four years. The study was published as a preprint , ahead of peer review. The researchers said the effects were not completely explained by weight loss, blood sugar control or inflammation. Study author Dr. Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, senior global director of cardiometabolic research and development at Novo Nordisk, said the benefits of GLP-1 medications had thus far been measured one disease at a time – but what if the effects were bigger than that? “If we’re touching so many diseases, are we actually also touching something that is systemic across these diseases? Is it aging? Is it health span?” he asked at the recent Aging Research and Drug Discovery meeting. Recent research in mice tried to answer some of these questions more directly. Mice typically live about two years, so it’s easier to follow them throughout their lifespan than it is to do the same for humans. Scientists at the University of California at Berkeley took 20-month-old mice – roughly the age equivalent of 60-year-old humans – and gave them injections of semaglutide or a placebo for the rest of their lives. They were roughly the same body weight at the start of the study. But the mice on semaglutide ate less and lost weight, and they lived longer than the mice that got placebo injections. The semaglutide-treated mice had an average lifespan of 834 days, about the same as 80 human years, while the mice injected with placebos lived 742 total days, or roughly 75 human years. To test whether it was the weight loss or the drug specifically that was responsible for the benefit, researchers next reduced the amount of calories fed to another group of mice by 25% — about the same amount of reduction seen in mice on semaglutide. Like the GLP-1-treated mice, the calorie-restricted mice lived longer, but there were some differences between the two groups, said Chen at UC Berkeley, who helped lead the research, which was published in the journal Nature . For many tissue functions the group looked at, especially related to muscle function and mobility, the semaglutide-treated mice and calorie-restricted mice performed about the same. But mice on semaglutide showed some advantages. They functioned better at thinking and at finding their way out of a maze, and they were better able to manage their blood sugar than mice on calorie restriction alone. “So that just means that it’s more than just a calorie restriction and has additional benefits,” Chen said.

title: No need for all men to worry about declining sperm counts. An expert explains
content: There are two times I see men get hyperfocused on their health: when they’re having issues with erections and when they’re having issues making babies. Those with fertility concerns tend to be younger and arrive with their partners. The concerns are different, but both can open the door to a bigger conversation about health. When an abnormal semen analysis or fertility concerns trigger a visit, I spend a lot of time sorting through things patients have heard about semen and general fertility. One fear they often mention is hearing that sperm counts are falling worldwide. Men and their partners worry less about why this is happening and more about what, if anything, they can do about it. The more I heard this concern, the more I started to think — are sperm counts really dropping worldwide? And wait. Should I, as a man, also be worried? Why are people talking about falling sperm counts? Alarms went off after a major global analysis published in 2022 estimated that average sperm concentration fell by about half between 1973 and 2018 among men not selected on the basis of fertility. The overall analysis combined 223 studies involving more than 57,000 men from 53 countries. This type of research, called a meta-analysis , combines results from multiple studies to look for an overall pattern. These analyses can strongly influence how doctors and patients understand an issue and what guidance to give the general population. Researchers estimated that average sperm concentration fell 51.6% and total sperm count fell 62.3%. Concentration measures the number of sperm per milliliter of semen, and total count measures the number in an entire ejaculate. These findings triggered alarms for researchers, doctors and patients. When you look at the numbers, these findings do appear alarming. The numbers also raise concerns about what might be affecting sperm production. For me and others in my field, they raised another question and opportunity — could sperm measurements give a window into a man’s overall health? I had a patient who was so stressed about dropping sperm counts that he worried about his future children and generations beyond. To him, the study sounded like a countdown to men no longer being able to reproduce. It’s a scary thought but goes beyond what the study can tell us. Other research also gives us reasons to question whether the same decline is happening everywhere. Sperm concentration showed no overall change in the initial analysis of samples collected from 1970 through 2018, according to a 2025 review and meta-analysis . It covered 58 studies involving 11,787 American men without known infertility issues. After adjusting for geographic region and fertility status, researchers found a modest annual decline in sperm concentration. In other words, the answer changed depending on whom was studied and how the numbers were analyzed. These findings do not negate the concern raised by the 2022 analysis. They do make the picture more complex than a single worldwide decline. For my worried patient, that study was not a countdown clock on his chance to become a dad. I told him what I am telling you — sperm counts are fine, for now. A doctor may commonly order a semen analysis as part of a fertility workup or after a vasectomy to ensure no sperm are left in the ejaculate. It can reveal a lot, but it cannot answer every question about fertility. The test measures several things, including how many sperm are present, how well they move and what percentage have a typical shape. The World Health Organization says its comparison numbers used to interpret the results should not be treated as an absolute line separating fertile from infertile men. Another complicating factor is that if a man dropped off a semen sample every day for a week, the numbers would not be the same each day. Length of abstinence, recent illness, medications, stress, collection conditions and differences among labs can all affect the results. It’s why the American Urological Association recommends at least two analyses, ideally a month apart, especially when the first result may be abnormal. I’ve seen men worry because their first test showed low motility, meaning the sperm were not moving well. I’ve also seen men with few or no sperm stay calm and simply ask, “OK, what can I do to improve this?” One test can indicate where to look. Repeated tests, interpreted alongside a medical history and examination, help make a plan. I once treated a patient whose sperm count and shape looked fine but whose motility, or ability to move, was poor. He exercised, did not smoke and barely drank. When we talked, he opened up about work stress and poor sleep. Six months later, after improving both, his sperm movement was better. He reported no other changes to his diet or lifestyle. Such a result does not prove better sleep and less stress caused the improvement. Semen results fluctuate. But his test results started a conversation about parts of his health that deserved attention regardless of whether his sperm improved. Most people hear sperm count and think about fertility and having kids. In my line of work, doctors see it as one part of a man’s broader health picture. Men with infertility or abnormal semen results have higher rates of some medical conditions, and urology guidelines recommend counseling them about that connection. An abnormal semen analysis is not a diagnosis of heart disease, diabetes or an early death. It is a reason to look under the hood: Check the man’s history, examine him, review medications and consider whether another health problem is being missed. Sperm health can be affected by some of the same conditions I discuss during a routine checkup, including medical issues, smoking, lack of sleep, heat and current medications. Science backs me up: Obesity, diabetes and metabolic syndrome were linked with poorer semen quality and damage to sperm DNA in a review of 112 studies . Men who slept less than six hours a night were about 40% less likely to get their partner pregnant in any given month compared with men who slept eight hours, according to a 2018 study of 1,176 couples . Cigarette smoking can affect semen quality. In one study of infertile heavy smokers , sperm concentration and total count improved three months after they quit. Lower sperm concentration and count were associated with exposure to heat waves in a study of men undergoing routine semen analysis in Argentina . The testicles sit outside the body for a reason. Sperm production works best below normal body temperature, and hence chronic heat exposure can interfere with that process. What about medications such as testosterone? I tell every man who wants children now or in the future to avoid testosterone replacement therapy. Guidelines warn that it can suppress sperm production, sometimes to zero. If symptoms of low testosterone are a concern, ask about alternate options that preserve fertility. Higher total testosterone levels were associated with GLP-1 drugs, according to a 2026 systematic review . Better semen measures in men with obesity or low testosterone have been reported in other studies. These findings are encouraging, but I am cautious about labeling or prescribing GLP-1 drugs as fertility drugs. These medications help men lose weight and manage chronic health conditions, which may then explain the benefits seen in testosterone and sperm quality. Whether these changes improve the chances of pregnancy still needs more study. When a man asks me if he should get on GLP-1 drugs, I encourage him to discuss whether they are appropriate for his weight and health conditions with his primary care doctor. My focus is on inspiring him to improve his overall health rather than prescribing a GLP-1 to help him make a baby. I also remind him that if he does become a father, taking care of himself now may help him stay healthy and active as his children grow. I start with one simple piece of advice: Do not panic over one result. If a semen analysis is abnormal, we will usually repeat it and look alongside your medical history. Some causes are treatable , and in some men, the workup can uncover more serious underlying health problems. Tell your doctor about medications, cannabis and any nicotine products you use. Knowing what you use helps doctors give you better advice. While we arrange more testing, I focus on the habits that support overall health: Do not smoke, avoid heavy drinking, exercise, work toward a healthy weight, get enough sleep and manage chronic conditions. Health habits start with what you’re eating. I tell guys all the time: If you love fast food, it’s probably not helping your fertility. A Mediterranean-style diet has been linked with better semen measures . Evidence that it improves the chances of pregnancy is less certain, so think long-term health plan, not quick fertility fix. You will also need to give your body time. Changes in habits or treatment take time to show up in sperm measurements, so there’s often a reassessment after about three months. Doing so is different from repeating an initial abnormal test to confirm the result period. A few days will not indicate whether a new routine is working. The worldwide debate over sperm counts will continue. In my office, the next step continues to be more personal. We’ll clear out any misconceptions, review results, address any issues we find, and build habits that support overall health and longevity. A fertility concern can be the start of taking better care of yourself, whether having children is in the plan or not.
